top_choice_rationale: P001 (Grossman and Helpman, with the citation confined to the political economy of trade protection) has the cleanest attribution on the slate. It is a long, tightly coupled two-person programme, so no one at the same level is excluded. The protection-for-sale framework made lobbying and tariff formation a precise, testable equilibrium object, which produced about three decades of theory, estimation and trade-agreement analysis. That maturity is not in doubt. The mixed, specification-sensitive empirical record is a real limit, so the citation should claim the framework and the research programme it created, not confirmed predictions. I also reject widening the citation to the growth strand, because that would stretch the discovery and invite an unverified overlap question with other prizes. P002 (Autor, Dorn, Hanson) is second. Its design-based evidence is strong and the three-name set is now stable, but the long-run persistence and shift-share identification debates are still open. P003 (Melitz and Helpman) is third. The firm-heterogeneity framework is influential and densely tested, but the exporter facts were established independently by uncredited originators, so attribution is weaker. A substantive award still ranks above no award, so P000 is last. I did not use the number of supporters as evidence of merit.
recusal_note: none apparent from profile. My profile lists no collaboration or institutional tie to Grossman, Helpman, Autor, Dorn, Hanson, Melitz, or any other credited name. P002 (B018) is close to my own field of empirical labour economics, which I disclose as field proximity and not as a basis for recusal. Hjalmarsson and I share Bertil Holmlund as a co-author, which is a link between committee members and not a candidate-specific conflict.
